# Parent Guide to Back-to-School Screen-Time Discussions


Practical Ways to Set Screen Rules Kids Will Actually Follow


By


Dr. Elizabeth Milovidov, Senior Director of Global Parental Advocacy


Published


Sep 15, 2026


As summer vacation winds down and kids head back to the classroom, parents everywhere are managing a transition to new routines. The days of sleeping in, extra screen time, and staying up later have come to a close, and kids (and parents) are adjusting to their new reality. For many households, that means taking a closer look at online gaming and other screen-time habits.


The good news is, parents don’t need to become tech experts to guide their kids through this shift. The shift back to school hours creates a natural opportunity for parents and caregivers to discuss healthy digital routines that support sleep, homework, learning, connection, and creativity. As an expert in digital parenting and education, I’m sharing a few practical strategies that can help families set realistic routines together; without turning screen time into a battle.


**1. Set new guidelines together.** Parental controls for things like screen time and spending limits can be helpful digital boundaries. But these are most effective when they’re part of an ongoing conversation between parents and kids. Letting kids actively participate in these decisions helps them learn how to self-regulate and teaches them to be digitally responsible, not just digitally restricted.


Decide together how much screen time is OK and when it’s time to shut down. For example, no screens during homework time, at dinner, at bedtime. Discuss a reasonable monthly budget for in-game purchases and have them help track it, and maybe even contribute some of their own allowance or pocket money. To set a good example, parents can agree to put their screens away during agreed-upon times, as well. Then write them down somewhere visible, like the fridge, so it’s a shared agreement everyone in the household can be held to.


**2. Explore their digital world with them.** Instead of monitoring from the sidelines, ask kids what they’re playing and who they’re playing with when they’re online. Let them become the teacher and share the games they like. Playing together builds trust, lets parents start to understand how their kids navigate online spaces, and opens the door to continuous, nonjudgmental conversations about healthy digital behavior.


Parents of younger children can use resources like Roblox’s[Family Zone](https://www.roblox.com/share-links?code=3f5491b8296f9d478979ce8b0f7ce412&type=ExperienceDetails&af_dp=roblox%3A%2F%2Fnavigation%2Fshare_links%3Fcode%3D3f5491b8296f9d478979ce8b0f7ce412%26type%3DExperienceDetails&deep_link_value=roblox%3A%2F%2Fnavigation%2Fshare_links%3Fcode%3D3f5491b8296f9d478979ce8b0f7ce412%26type%3DExperienceDetails&pid=ExperienceDetails&is_retargeting=false) , a game specifically designed to teach parents and caregivers about the games and settings available for families. For older kids, walk through their settings and give them a chance to explain what’s important to them. For example, they may want more time in the late evening because that’s when their friends are online and they want to play together.


**3. Help them develop important life skills.** The right time to begin discussing online safety is as soon as a child begins using technology. Discussing and setting boundaries for their digital life can be the subtext for teaching children how to manage their time and take ownership of their routines in all areas of their lives. Focus on empowering them with digital literacy, so they make smart, safe decisions even when they don’t have an adult in the room, looking over their shoulder.


Arm them with clear strategies ahead of time, so they know exactly what to do if a stranger tries to contact them in any online setting or someone asks them to move to a different site to chat. Talk about how to use reporting tools, and let them know they can come discuss it openly and make decisions together.


If they push boundaries or break the online rules that were set, approach it the same as real-life rule-breaking; with appropriate, calm consequences. Ask them why they felt they had to bypass the rules, work on a compromise together, and focus on rebuilding trust. Visit our[parenting guides](https://about.roblox.com/parent-resources) for more information about navigating these conversations.


**4. Focus on behavior over minutes.** Watch how kids act. Are they sleeping and eating well? Are they doing well in school? Are they behaving respectfully to caregivers, siblings, and teachers? Are they interacting well with friends? If all of these answers are yes, there likely is not a screen issue. The time to step in is when behavior seems to be changing. Talk to them about what’s changed and why, and decide together if online rules need to be adjusted. The[guide to gaming and mental health](https://about.roblox.com/pdf/gamin-mental-health) can help them understand some of the changes they might notice in themselves or others.


**5. Remember that all screen time isn’t the same.** Sitting alone scrolling an endless feed is different from creating, collaborating, or playing with friends even when that’s online rather than in person. The best way to understand exactly how kids are spending their screen time (and why it’s fun for them) is a real conversation.


Gaming with friends may provide opportunities for learning, creativity, and collaboration. On Roblox, kids could be learning how to code or design or expressing themselves by trying out new looks with their avatar. As kids get older, screens may become part of their schoolwork. By taking the time to understand the different homework apps, online research, and class communications tools their kids are expected to use, parents can distinguish productive, required screen time from play or social use.


Finally, remember that kids are always learning by watching what the adults around them are doing. Adults can be aware of their own screen usage and create device-free zones and moments (e.g., no screens at the dinner table). Let kids know that adults also have to set limits and sometimes overdo it, and tell them what that feels like (headache, grumpy, etc.). That may help them recognize the signs themselves and realize when it’s time to put the device away. A new school year is a natural moment to build these habits as a family, so that the time you have together stays time you actually spend with each other.
